abstract: In the version of the article initially published, in the “Oxylipin genes” panel of Fig. 5e, there were two “4 days” labels in the “COM” section. The right label has now been corrected to “8 days” in the HTML and PDF versions of the article.

title: Establishing Polycomb regulatory landscapes in human early development
abstract: H2AK119ub (H2Aub) and H3K27me3, which are deposited by the Polycomb group (PcG) complexes PRC1 and PRC2, respectively, cooperatively repress developmental genes. However, in human preimplantation embryos, H3K27me3 undergoes genome-wide erasure and subsequent restoration. How H3K27me3 is reestablished and whether PcG complexes still regulate gene repression in human embryos remain unknown. Here, we profiled H2Aub dynamics from human gametes to blastocysts. H2Aub emerges in GC-rich regions as early as the two-cell stage, progressively accumulates at both active and inactive genes, and further culminates at PcG targets in later stages. H3K27me3 is weakly correlated with H2Aub in oocytes and two-cell embryos but colocalizes with H2Aub at H3K4me3-depleted, inactive PcG targets in blastocysts. Loss of H2Aub abolishes H3K27me3 reestablishment at PcG targets causing moderate derepression, accompanied by ectopic H3K27me3 deposition and impaired embryonic development. Finally, H2Aub and DNA methylation cooperatively maintain H3K27me3 patterning in human embryonic stem cells. Therefore, H2Aub-dependent H3K27me3 deposition underlies the earliest establishment of Polycomb repression in humans.

title: RNA ends connect genetic risk to brain disease
abstract: Alternative polyadenylation changes mRNA ends, thereby altering mRNA stability, translation or subcellular localization without necessarily changing RNA abundance. New work mapping this post-transcriptional layer across 379 human brains shows how genetic variation in 3′-UTR choice relates to disease-associated loci and downstream molecular effects.

title: A systems perspective on monoallelic inborn errors of immunity
abstract: The genetic architecture of inborn errors of immunity continues to grow in complexity, exposing the limitations of variant-centric concepts that have long shaped the field. While complete loss-of-function genotypes have been instrumental in defining essential gene functions in human immunity and inflammation, they have also entrenched binary interpretations of causality that fail to account for pleiotropy, variable expressivity and incomplete penetrance—especially in monoallelic disease. Monoallelic variants often perturb signaling rather than abolishing it. The integration of these perturbations into molecular and cellular systems, and eventually immune circuits, governs phenotypic expression. Here, we revisit and extend classic concepts of genetic dominance and genetic pleiotropy and suggest that these are not sole properties of alleles but emerge from the complex and dynamic behavior of molecular, cellular and immune systems to buffer genetic variance.

title: Imputation of fluid intelligence to increase power for gene discovery
abstract: A study imputes fluid intelligence from correlated variables to expand the UK Biobank analysis sample from around 285,000 to 455,000 individuals, boosting discovery of both common and rare genetic variants and charting a roadmap for imputing phenotypes while minimizing bias in future gene-discovery studies.

title: Multiancestry conditional and joint analysis applied to GWAS summary statistics
abstract: Conditional and joint (COJO) analysis of genome-wide association study (GWAS) data is a standard post-GWAS analysis for identifying statistically independent associations. Although GWAS meta-analyses are increasingly conducted across multiple ancestry groups, the optimal strategy for multiancestry COJO analysis remains unclear. Here we introduce Manc-COJO, a method for multiancestry COJO analysis. Simulations and real-data analyses show that Manc-COJO improves detection of independent association signals while reducing false positives compared with single-ancestry COJO implemented in genome-wide complex trait analysis (GCTA) and its ad-hoc multiancestry adaptations. We also introduce Manc-COJO:FIX, a follow-up algorithm to identify ancestry-specific independent associations. The C++ implementation of Manc-COJO is over 120-fold faster than GCTA-COJO and supports linkage disequilibrium references derived from either individual-level genotype data or pre-computed matrices, facilitating analyses when data sharing is limited.

title: The landscape of gene loss and missense variation across the mammalian tree informs on gene essentiality
abstract: Patterns of gene and sequence preservation across species provide insight into gene essentiality under natural selection. Here we developed two interspecies constraint metrics across 462 mammalian species: Gene Identity Score of Mammalian Orthologs (GISMO), which quantifies gene loss weighted by evolutionary distance to humans, and GISMO-mis, which measures missense constraint using the ratio of missense to synonymous variation across mammals. Both metrics are strongly correlated with human loss of function, missense and dosage constraint derived from large-scale sequencing studies, yet are largely independent of coding sequence length. GISMO and GISMO-mis identify essential genes missed by existing human-only metrics, particularly short genes. Genes in the most constrained deciles are enriched for rare variant associations in disorders linked to reduced fecundity, including schizophrenia, autism and neurodevelopmental disorders, and show strong enrichment for common variant heritability. These deciles also exhibit reduced copy number variation, consistent with dosage sensitivity. In addition, GISMO improves prioritization of recessive disease genes and captures signatures of homozygous selection across the mammalian tree. Taken together, GISMO and GISMO-mis leverage deep mammalian evolution to provide complementary, length-robust measures of gene essentiality that strengthen disease–gene prioritization and illuminate the selective forces shaping human biology.

title: Genome-wide analyses identify 60 loci associated with liver triglyceride content
abstract: We performed a large-scale genome-wide association study meta-analysis of magnetic resonance imaging-derived liver triglyceride content across 71,488 European-ancestry participants from the UK Biobank, approximately doubling the sample size of previous genome-wide association studies 1 . We identified 60 independent loci, including 31 not previously reported, and estimated the single nucleotide polymorphism-based heritability of liver triglyceride content at 25%. Integrative fine-mapping and gene-prioritization analyses nominated candidate effector genes for 48 loci. Of the 31 newly identified variants, 14 were validated in meta-analyses of clinically diagnosed metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (42,163 cases and 1,646,254 controls). People in the highest versus lowest decile of a polygenic risk score for liver triglyceride content had 2.71-fold higher odds of cirrhosis and 7.47-fold higher odds of hepatocellular carcinoma. Plasma proteins associated with the liver triglyceride polygenic risk score were enriched for metabolic remodeling and inflammatory pathways, with liver-enriched protein signatures increasing and visceral adipose signatures decreasing with higher genetic risk. Together, these findings refine the genetic architecture of liver triglyceride content, linking polygenic susceptibility to downstream metabolic and inflammatory pathways and providing insights into the genetic basis of steatotic liver disease.

title: Leveraging genomic deep learning models for the prediction of noncoding variant effects
abstract: Characterizing noncoding variant function remains an important challenge in human genetics. Genomic deep learning models have emerged as a promising approach to enable in silico prediction of variant effects. These models include supervised sequence-to-activity models, which predict molecular phenotypes such as genome-wide chromatin states or gene expression levels directly from DNA sequence, and self-supervised genomic language models. Here we review progress in leveraging these models for noncoding variant effect prediction. We describe practical considerations for making such predictions and categorize the types of ground-truth data used to evaluate variant effect predictions, providing insight into the settings in which current models are most useful. Our Review highlights key considerations for practitioners and opportunities for improvement in model development and evaluation.

title: Genome-wide detection of genotype–environment interactions at biobank scale with fastGxE
abstract: Traditional genome-wide association studies have primarily focused on detecting main genotype effects, often overlooking genotype–environment interactions (GxE), which are essential for understanding context-specific genetic effects and refining disease etiology. Here we present fast genotype–environment interaction analysis (fastGxE), a scalable and effective genome-wide GxE method designed to identify genetic variants that interact with environmental factors to influence traits of interest. fastGxE controls for polygenic effects, polygenic interaction effects and noise heterogeneity; it remains robust to the number of environmental factors involved in GxE interactions; and it ensures scalability for genome-wide GxE analysis in large biobank studies, achieving speed improvements of 32.98–126.49 times over existing approaches. We illustrate the benefits of fastGxE through extensive simulations and an in-depth analysis of 32 physical traits and 67 blood biomarkers from the UK Biobank. In real-data applications, fastGxE identifies 7 genomic loci associated with physical traits, including 4 novel ones, and 18 genomic loci associated with blood biomarkers, 12 of which are novel. The new discoveries highlight the dynamic interplay between genetics and the environment, uncovering potentially clinically relevant pathways that could inform personalized interventions and treatment strategies.

title: Near-complete assembly of wild emmer wheat unveils centromere reorganization during polyploid evolution
abstract: Wild emmer wheat ( Triticum turgidum ssp. dicoccoides , BBAA), the wild progenitor of cultivated tetraploid and hexaploid wheats, provides an important reference for investigating centromere reorganization during polyploidization and domestication. Here we generated a near-complete genome assembly of wild emmer wheat, including centromeric regions for all 14 centromeres. Comparative analyses with cultivated tetraploid and hexaploid wheats revealed extensive variation in centromere-associated sequences and centromere-proximal structure, as well as distinct subgenome-associated patterns in the A and B subgenomes. The A subgenome was characterized by positional shifts and sequence turnover of CRW-rich centromere-derived blocks, whereas the B subgenome showed reduced CentT566 satellite abundance accompanied by localized retention or expansion on specific chromosomes. These results provide a high-resolution tetraploid wheat reference and reveal subgenome-associated patterns of centromere remodeling during wheat polyploid evolution.

title: High false sign rates in transcriptome-wide association studies
abstract: Transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) are widely used to identify genes involved in complex traits and to infer the direction of gene effects on traits. However, despite their popularity, it remains unclear how accurately TWAS recover the true direction of a gene’s effect on a trait. Here we estimate the false sign rate of TWAS for plasma proteins, leveraging the expectation that increased gene expression should generally increase protein expression. We then extend this framework to complex traits, where loss-of-function burden tests provide the expected direction of effect. In both analyses, we observe high discordance with expectations, with TWAS showing a false sign rate of 23% for plasma proteins and 33% for complex traits. We propose that much of the sign discordance arises when expression quantitative trait loci in non-trait-relevant tissues tag haplotypes associated with traits in genome-wide association studies via distinct, tightly linked regulatory variants, yielding spurious TWAS associations with the correct genes but with unreliable direction of effect. These findings show that TWAS-based direction-of-effect estimates should be interpreted with caution and raise concerns about the reliability of TWAS more broadly.

title: Co-regulation confounds direction of genetic effects in transcriptome-wide association studies
abstract: Co-regulation of gene expression profiles across cell types arising from linkage disequilibrium makes it challenging to distinguish causal variants from nearby tagging variants. A study now quantifies the effect of this confounding factor on the direction of the gene–disease association in transcriptome-wide association studies.

title: Quantification method affects replicability of eQTL analysis, colocalization and TWAS
abstract: Expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) mapping, colocalization and transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) are widely used to contextualize genome-wide association study loci, yet the impact of upstream RNA-sequencing processing choices on these analyses remains critically unexplored. Two poorly characterized decisions include the transcriptomic reference annotation used for quantification of short-read RNA-sequencing samples, which defines transcript composition and structure, and the quantification method itself. Here, through a comprehensive analysis spanning 48 tissues in GTEx and 7 widely studied and diverse phenotypes, we find that these choices substantially affect eQTL detection and gene expression prediction with significant downstream impacts on colocalization and TWAS results. Concordant results across pipelines are further enriched for longer genes, genes with more isoforms, and greater expression heritability. Our findings demonstrate that seemingly minor methodological decisions substantially affect these common analyses, highlighting the need for standardized practices to ensure reproducible genetic association studies.

title: Interferon-α directs hematopoietic stem cells toward competing fates
abstract: Chronic inflammation drives clonal hematopoietic expansions, yet IFNα depletes clones in myeloproliferative neoplasms. A new study tackles this paradox, revealing that IFNα induces competing trajectories whose balance ultimately determines clonal fate: depletion or persistence.

title: fastGxE is a powerful method for uncovering genotype–environment interactions in biobanks
abstract: fastGxE is a scalable and powerful method that accelerates genome-wide scans for genotype–environment interactions in biobank datasets. When applied to the UK Biobank, fastGxE identified previously uncharacterized genotype–environment interaction loci for physical traits and routinely assayed blood biomarkers, revealing context-dependent genetic effects.

title: The Gujarat Tribal Genome Project (2kTGP)
Population-scale single-nucleus multi-omic profiling of skeletal muscle reveals extensive context-specific genetic regulation
abstract: Skeletal muscle tissue underlies several polygenic metabolic traits and diseases. Identifying their genetic mechanisms requires pinpointing cell types, regulatory elements, target genes and causal variants. Here we use genetic multiplexing to generate population-scale single-nucleus chromatin accessibility (single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (snATAC–seq)) and transcriptome (single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq)) maps across 287 frozen human skeletal muscle biopsies. We identify 13 cell types and integrate genetic variation to discover >7,000 expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) and >100,000 chromatin accessibility QTLs (caQTLs) across cell types, including context-specific eQTL/caQTL with significant G × C interaction. We identify nearly 2,000 eGenes colocalized with caQTL and construct causal directional maps for chromatin accessibility and gene expression. Almost 3,500 genome-wide association study (GWAS) signals across 38 relevant traits colocalize with sn-eQTL/caQTL, most in a cell-specific manner. These signals typically colocalize with caQTL and not eQTL, highlighting the importance of population-scale chromatin profiling for GWAS functional studies. The results of this study illuminate the genetic regulatory architecture of human skeletal muscle.

title: A haplotype reference panel constructed from 490,319 UK Biobank genomes improves genotype imputation for global populations
abstract: Here we constructed a genotype imputation reference panel from whole-genome sequencing data from 490,319 UK Biobank (UKB) participants 1 and enabled both standalone and cloud-based phasing and imputation through EagleImp 2 and EagleImp-RAP within the UK Biobank Research Analysis Platform. The UKB reference panel achieves lower phasing switch error rates than the widely used TOPMed r3 panel (133,597 individuals) for all global superpopulations except AMR and for 25 of 26 1000 Genomes Project subpopulations. Imputation accuracy, measured by MAE, improved for 4 of 5 superpopulations and 12 subpopulations for variants with minor allele frequencies down to 0.01%. Estimated squared correlation further improved across all 5 superpopulations and 22 subpopulations, with the largest gains in East and South Asian populations. Reimputation of COVID-19 genome-wide association study datasets from Italy, Germany, Spain and Norway 3 , 4 demonstrated that common-variant imputation remains unsaturated, enhancing the discovery of genome-wide significant loci and improving fine-mapping resolution.

title: Ethical challenges in patient-focused drug development for rare genetic diseases
abstract: Patient and family groups increasingly drive the development of drugs for rare diseases, from trial design to regulatory strategy. This model of patient-focused drug development can accelerate therapies for rare diseases but also generates recurring ethical tensions with academic, industry and regulatory partners that remain underdiscussed.

title: A catalog of transcriptome genetic regulation in a consanguineous Middle Eastern biobank
abstract: Ancestry-specific genetic mapping of transcriptome regulation is pivotal for understanding genome function, especially in underrepresented consanguineous populations. Here we characterized 1,882 Qatar Biobank participants, integrating blood RNA sequencing, whole-genome sequencing and phenotypic data across 45 clinically relevant traits. We cataloged ~7 million significant quantitative trait loci (QTLs), both short and structural variants, impacting gene expression, isoform usage, splicing and allele-specific expression, uncovering 1,379 novel eGenes. Fine-mapping resolved 29,953 high-confidence, independent causal loci including 24% previously unreported as well as those with effect alleles showing significant divergence across global populations, while 1,371 were absent from public databases. Leveraging elevated autozygosity, we found that causal variants are depleted from runs of homozygosity, consistent with purifying selection, while recent autozygosity increased the burden of homozygous regulatory variants. We identified QTLs with recessive deleterious effects on 10 Mendelian disease genes and homozygous QTLs causing extreme outlier expression in 66 genes including dosage-sensitive ones. Colocalization analysis revealed 58 causal variants acting on 20 clinically relevant phenotypes, implicating novel genes including ATP6V0B and RQCD1 in metabolic and blood disorders. These findings establish this QTL catalog as a valuable Middle Eastern resource for genome interpretation and genomic medicine.

title: Clonal hematopoiesis and cytopenias following CAR19 therapy
abstract: CD19-directed chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapy (CAR19) improves survival in relapsed/refractory large B cell lymphoma compared with immunochemotherapy with intent for autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (autoHCT). However, major toxicities include prolonged cytopenias, infection and secondary hematologic malignancies. Here, to investigate these complications, we studied patients with lymphoma receiving CAR19 and compared clinical outcomes to propensity-matched autoHCT-treated controls. CAR19-treated patients exhibited impaired immune reconstitution and increased infection. Bone marrow analysis showed that prolonged post-CAR cytopenias are associated with clonal cytopenias of undetermined significance and interferon-mediated inflammation. Clonal hematopoiesis (CH) commonly expanded following CAR19 infusion and was associated with impaired immune reconstitution and treatment-related myeloid malignancy (tMN). Post-CAR tMN was molecularly and clinically comparable to post-autoHCT tMN. Single-cell DNA analysis revealed mostly independent CH clones, while CAR integration into CH-mutant T cells occurred frequently and may drive expansion and persistence. Together, these findings implicate CH expansion and marrow inflammation in key CAR19-associated toxicities.

title: A framework for genome-wide characterization of DNA methylation and variant effect prediction
abstract: DNA methylation plays a critical role in many essential biological processes, including transcriptional regulation, genomic imprinting, chromosomal maintenance, genomic stability and development, and has phenotypic and disease impacts. However, genome-wide characterization of methylation patterns across cell types and tissues remains a major challenge. Here, to address this, we present a framework that enables systematic genome-wide analysis of methylation and sequence-based prediction of context-specific methylation effects of variants. Our data-driven discovery of methylation classes reveals context-dependent roles for methylation across tissues, cell types and regions of the genome. The framework also includes Wreath, a deep learning-based sequence model specifically designed to accurately predict the context-dependent impact of any genetic variant on methylation. These developments leverage a compendium that harmonizes disparate methylation profiles from disparate studies including over 90 tissues and cell types. Using Wreath, we systematically characterized the impact of noncoding pathogenic variants on tissue-specific methylation, generating mechanistic hypotheses for individual regulatory variants. We make the full framework, including the compendium, the methylation classes and the model, available for use by the community.

title: Hematotoxicity: the hidden legacy of CAR T cell therapy
abstract: CD19-directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy can produce durable remission in patients with lymphoma, but persistent hematological toxicities remain poorly understood. We show that clonal expansion of mutated hematopoietic clones (clonal hematopoiesis) in an inflamed bone marrow environment is linked to prolonged cytopenias, impaired immune recovery and treatment-related myeloid malignancies.

title: Progress and disparities in fungal genomics in the long-read era
abstract: Fungal genomics has expanded rapidly over the past three decades, yet this growth has been phylogenetically uneven and many taxonomic gaps persist. Here we review the field from early efforts such as the Fungal Genome Initiative to the current era of third-generation long-read sequencing and compile publicly available assemblies to quantify trends in contiguity, completeness, long-read adoption and taxonomic representation. We argue that fungal genomics has moved from a period of data scarcity to one in which the principal constraints are taxonomic bias, inconsistent annotation, sparse metadata and the interpretation of complex genome structure. Substantial phylogenetic gaps remain, particularly outside Dikarya and among unculturable taxa, and only a minority of assemblies are annotated. We therefore identify priorities for the fungal community, including coordinated efforts to close major taxonomic gaps, improved repository metrics to facilitate the identification of high-quality assemblies and standardized genome annotation, which is lacking for most assemblies.

title: AI-based precision prognostics and therapy personalization for childhood brain tumors
abstract: Accurate prediction of patient outcomes remains a critical challenge in oncology, in particular for childhood brain tumors, in which treatment decisions need to carefully balance risk of tumor recurrence and death against severe therapy-induced sequelae. Here, we developed MANTIS ( m ethylation profiling and a rtificial n eural networks for t ime-dependent i ndividualized s urvival predictions), a precision artificial intelligence (AI) tool for medulloblastoma and ependymoma outcome prediction built on genome-wide DNA methylation array data from 2,786 patients. MANTIS generates individualized survival probabilities over a 10-year period and achieves concordance indices as high as 0.80 ± 0.07, significantly exceeding the predictive accuracy of current clinical indicators. Extending MANTIS to estimate individualized treatment effects identifies ~60% of patients with average-risk medulloblastoma without a significant survival disadvantage ( P = 0.683) when treated with less intensive craniospinal irradiation doses, which is associated with improved neurocognitive outcomes. In conclusion, our study establishes a foundation for AI-based precision prognostics and therapy personalization in childhood brain tumors and offers a blueprint for similar initiatives in other cancer types.

title: Longitudinal single-cell profiling of breast tumors highlights immune and epigenetic mechanisms associated with sensitivity to aromatase inhibitors
abstract: Estrogen receptor (ER)-positive breast cancer treatment is based primarily on endocrine therapy. To dissect mechanisms of sensitivity to aromatase inhibitors in ER-positive breast cancer, we profiled tumor biopsies from 25 patients during neoadjuvant therapy using single-cell RNA sequencing, immune receptor sequencing and enhancer activity mapping. Malignant cells with high ER signaling and elevated activity of enhancers with ER binding sites were sensitive to treatment. Resistance was associated with androgen receptor signaling, dedifferentiation and epithelial–mesenchymal transition. Poor responders preferentially used the androgen receptor cis -regulome under treatment pressure. The baseline tumor microenvironment was associated with tumor downstaging. Poor responders exhibited a ‘hot’, yet ineffective immune landscape enriched for naive lymphoid and undifferentiated myeloid cells. Good responders showed an active immune microenvironment with sustained clonal expansion of T cells. Our longitudinal single-cell analyses elucidate the genetic, cellular and epigenetic mechanisms driving sensitivity and resistance to neoadjuvant aromatase inhibition in ER-positive breast cancer.

title: The Participant Engagement and Cancer Genome Sequencing Network to accelerate research in rare and understudied cancers
authors: On behalf of the Participant Engagement and Cancer Genome Sequencing (PE-CGS) Network
abstract: The genomic characterization of cancers has considerably advanced research and clinical practice. However, critical gaps remain, including limited knowledge of tumor profiles in rare cancers and populations understudied in genomic research and insufficient integration of genomic, clinical and epidemiologic data. This Perspective highlights the Participant Engagement and Cancer Genome Sequencing (PE-CGS) Network, established by the US National Cancer Institute to address knowledge gaps in rare and understudied cancers. PE-CGS comprises five research centers supported by a coordinating center and guided by an external advisory panel. Collaborations across PE-CGS are grounded in shared values of participant-centeredness, engagement, access, collaboration and innovation. Activities emphasize participant engagement throughout the research process, including the return of results and collection of clinical and epidemiologic data alongside paired tumor/germline sequencing. PE-CGS demonstrates how engagement, return of results and comprehensive data collection can be integrated to support participant-centered cancer genomics research and accelerate research in rare and understudied cancers.
